definition: The National Firearms Act of 1934 (NFA), codified at 26 U.S.C. §§ 5801-5872 was the first major federal law to impose significant restrictions on certain categories of firearms. Congress enacted the NFA against the backdrop of Prohibition-era gang violence and the use of certain firearms in organized crime, including the St. Valentine’s Day Massacre in 1929. The attempted assassination of President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1933 also contributed to the political climate surrounding federal firearms legislation, although the NFA's legislative history is more directly associated with efforts to address mob violence and the use of machineguns, silencers, and sawed-off shotguns. The NFA was enacted pursuant to Congress's taxing power and imposed taxes and regulatory requirements on certain firearms rather than establishing a general federal prohibition on their possession. The law imposed taxes on the manufacture and transfer of covered firearms and required their registration with the federal government. The transfer tax was intended to discourage or eliminate transactions of certain firearms that Congress viewed as particularly associated with crime. Under 26 U.S.C. § 5845(a) , the term “firearm” for purposes of the NFA includes:  a shotgun having a barrel or barrels of less than 18 inches in length;  a weapon made from a shotgun if such weapon as modified has an overall length of less than 26 inches or a barrel or barrels of less than 18 inches in length;  a rifle having a barrel or barrels of less than 16 inches in length;  a weapon made from a rifle if such weapon as modified has an overall length of less than 26 inches or a barrel or barrels of less than 16 inches in length;  any other weapon, as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 5845(e);  a machinegun;  any silencer (as defined in 18 U.S.C. § 921(a)(25); and  a destructive device. The U.S. Supreme Court addressed the constitutionality of the NFA in United States v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174 (1939). This case involved a Second Amendment challenge to the NFA as applied to a 12-gauge shotgun with a barrel less than 18 inches long.
